'''Peter John Hilton''' (7 April 1923<ref name="all-sorts">Peter Hilton, "On all Sorts of Automorphisms", ''[[The American Mathematical Monthly]]'', 92(9), November 1985, p. 650</ref>{{spaced ndash}}6 November 2010<ref>{{Citation | title = Obituaries: Peter Hilton | date = 8 November 2010 | url = http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/pressconnects/obituary.aspx?n=peter-hilton&pid=146500873 | accessdate = 9 November 2010 }}</ref>) was a British mathematician, noted for his contributions to [[homotopy theory]] and for [[Cryptanalysis|code-breaking]] during [[World War II]].<ref>{{cite journal|last=Pedersen|first= Jean|authorlink=Jean Pedersen|title=Peter Hilton: Code Breaker and Mathematician (1923–2010)|journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]]|year=2011|volume=58|issue=11|pages=1538–1540|url=https://www.ams.org/notices/201111/rtx111101538p.pdf|mr=2896083}}</ref>

==Early life==
He was born in [[Brondesbury]], London, the son of Mortimer Jacob Hilton (1893–1959),<ref name=Mortimer-Jacob-Hilton>{{cite web|title=Erdberg later Hilton, Mordechai later Mortimer Jacob|website=british-jewry.org.uk|url=https://british-jewry.org.uk/leedsjewry/getperson.php?personID=I0044363&tree=1}}</ref> a Jewish physician who was in general practice in [[Peckham]], and his wife Elizabeth Amelia Freedman (1900–1984),<ref name=Mortimer-Jacob-Hilton/> and was brought up in [[Kilburn, London|Kilburn]].<ref name="ODNB">{{cite ODNB |id=102834 |last1 = James |first1 = I. M. |authorlink=Ioan James |title = Hilton, Peter John (1923–2010)}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Jewish Personnel at Bletchley Park in World War II |url=https://www.jewishvirtuallibrary.org/jewish-personnel-at-bletchley-park-in-world-war-ii |website=www.jewishvirtuallibrary.org}}</ref> The physiologist Sidney Montague Hilton (1921–2011) of the [[University of Birmingham Medical School]] was his elder brother.<ref>{{cite web |title=Sidney Montague Hilton 17 March 1921–28 January 2011 |url=https://static.physoc.org/app/uploads/2019/02/22200714/Hilton-full-obituary.pdf |website=static.physoc.org|pages=62–63}}</ref>

Hilton was educated at [[St Paul's School, London]].<ref name="bp-about">"About the speaker", [http://www.nationalcodescentre.org/edu/lectures/turing.rhtm announcement] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070222093557/http://www.nationalcodescentre.org/edu/lectures/turing.rhtm |date=22 February 2007 }} of a lecture given by Peter Hilton at Bletchley Park on 12 July 2006. Retrieved 18 January 2007.</ref><ref>{{Cite news | url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2010/dec/02/peter-hilton-obituary | title=Peter Hilton obituary| newspaper=[[The Guardian]]| date=2 December 2010| last1=Stewart| first1=Ian |author-link=Ian Stewart (mathematician)}}</ref><ref name="ODNB"/> He went to [[The Queen's College, Oxford]] in 1940 to read mathematics, on an open scholarship, where the mathematics tutor was Ughtred Haslam-Jones.<ref name="bp-about"/><ref name="ODNB"/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Titchmarsh |first1=E. C. |author-link=Edward Charles Titchmarsh |title=Ughtred Shuttleworth Haslam-Jones {{!}} Titchmarsh, E. C. {{!}} download |journal=Journal of the London Mathematical Society |date=1963 |volume=s1-38 |issue=1 |url=https://ur.booksc.eu/book/21131716/264617}}</ref>

==Bletchley Park==
A wartime undergraduate at [[Oxford University|Oxford]], on a shortened course, Hilton was obliged to train with the [[Royal Artillery]], and faced scheduled [[conscription]] in summer 1942.<ref name="lwf-190">Peter Hilton, "Living with Fish: Breaking Tunny in the Newmanry and the Testery", p. 190 from pp. 189–203 in [[Jack Copeland]] ed, ''Colossus: The Secrets of [[Bletchley Park]]'s Codebreaking Computers'', [[Oxford University Press]], 2006.</ref> After four terms, he took the advice of his tutor, and followed up a civil service recruitment contact.<ref name="ODNB"/> He had an interview for mathematicians with knowledge of German, and was offered a position in the [[Foreign Office]] without being told the nature of the work. The team was, in fact, recruiting on behalf of the [[Government Communications Headquarters#Government Code and Cypher School|Government Code and Cypher School]]. Aged 18, he arrived at the [[codebreaking]] station [[Bletchley Park]] on 12 January 1942.<ref>Hilton, "Living with Fish", p. 189</ref>

Hilton worked with several of the Bletchley Park deciphering groups. He was initially assigned to Naval [[Enigma machine|Enigma]] in [[Hut 8]]. Hilton commented on his experience working with [[Alan Turing]], whom he knew well for the last 12 years of his life, in his "Reminiscences of Bletchley Park" from ''A Century of Mathematics in America:''<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ams.org/publicoutreach/math-history/hmath1-hilton22.pdf|title=A Century of Mathematics in America, Part 1, Reminiscences of Bletchley Park|last=Hilton|first=Peter|website=}}</ref>{{quote|It is a rare experience to meet an authentic genius. Those of us privileged to inhabit the world of scholarship are familiar with the intellectual stimulation furnished by talented colleagues. We can admire the ideas they share with us and are usually able to understand their source; we may even often believe that we ourselves could have created such concepts and originated such thoughts. However, the experience of sharing the intellectual life of a genius is entirely different; one realizes that one is in the presence of an intelligence, a sensibility of such profundity and originality that one is filled with wonder and excitement.|sign=|source=}} Hilton echoed similar thoughts in the Nova [[PBS]] documentary ''Decoding Nazi Secrets'' (UK ''Station X'', Channel 4, 1999).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/nova/transcripts/2615decoding.html|title=NOVA, Transcripts, Decoding Nazi Secrets, PBS|publisher=PBS|access-date=29 August 2019}}</ref>

In late 1942, Hilton transferred to work on German [[teleprinter]] ciphers.<ref name="lwf-190"/> A special section known as the "[[Testery]]" had been formed in July 1942 to work on one such cipher, codenamed "[[Lorenz cipher|Tunny]]", and Hilton was one of the early members of the group.<ref name="roberts">[[Jerry Roberts]], "Major Tester's Section", p. 250 of pp. 249–259 in Jack Copeland ed, ''Colossus: The Secrets of Bletchley Park's Codebreaking Computers'', Oxford University Press, 2006.</ref> His role was to devise ways to deal with changes in Tunny, and to liaise with another section working on Tunny, the "[[Newmanry]]", which complemented the hand-methods of the Testery with specialised codebreaking machinery.<ref name="roberts"/> Hilton has been counted as a member of the Newmanry, possibly on a part-time basis.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Reeds |first1=James A. |last2=Diffie |first2=Whitfield |last3=Field |first3=J. V. |author-link3=Judith V. Field|title=Breaking Teleprinter Ciphers at Bletchley Park: An edition of I.J. Good, D. Michie and G. Timms: General Report on Tunny with Emphasis on Statistical Methods (1945) |date=7 July 2015 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |isbn=978-0-470-46589-9 |page=553 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2-tyCQAAQBAJ&pg=PA553 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Recreational ===
A convivial pub drinker at Bletchley Park, Hilton also spent time with Turing working on [[chess problem]]s and [[palindromes]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sugarman |first1=Martin |title=A supplement to 'Breaking the codes: Jewish personnel at Bletchley Park' |journal=Jewish Historical Studies |date=2011 |volume=43 |page=219 |jstor=29780153 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/29780153 |issn=0962-9696}}</ref> He there constructed a 51-letter palindrome:<ref>[[I. J. Good|Jack Good]], "Enigma and Fish", p. 160 from pp. 149–166 in F. H. Hinsley and Alan Strip, editors, ''Codebreakers: The Inside Story of Bletchley Park'', 1993.</ref> <blockquote>"Doc note, I dissent. A fast never prevents a fatness. I diet on cod."</blockquote>

==Mathematics==
[[File:Eckmann Hilton Serre Haefliger.jpg|thumb|[[Beno Eckmann]], Peter Hilton, [[Jean-Pierre Serre]], and [[André Haefliger]] in [[Zürich]] in 2007]]
Hilton obtained his [[Doctor of Philosophy|DPhil]] in 1949 from [[Oxford University]] under the supervision of [[J. H. C. Whitehead|John Henry Whitehead]]. His dissertation was "Calculation of the homotopy groups of <math>A_n^2</math>-polyhedra".<ref name="mathgen">{{MathGenealogy |id=6773}}</ref><ref name="interview">David Joyner and David Kahn, editors, "Edited Transcript of Interview with Peter Hilton for ''Secrets of War''", in ''[[Cryptologia]]'' 30(3), July–September 2006, pp. 236–250.</ref> His principal research interests were in [[algebraic topology]], [[homological algebra]], categorical algebra and mathematics education. He published 15 books and over 600 articles in these areas, some jointly with colleagues. [[Hilton's theorem]] (1955) is on the [[homotopy group]]s of a [[Wedge sum|wedge]] of [[sphere]]s. It addresses an issue that comes up in the theory of "homotopy operations".<ref>{{cite book |last1=Whitehead |first1=George W. |title=Elements of Homotopy Theory |date=6 December 2012 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-1-4612-6318-0 |page=xiii |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xEDaBwAAQBAJ&pg=PR13 |language=en}}</ref>

Turing, at the [[Victoria University of Manchester]], in 1948 invited Hilton to see the [[Manchester Mark 1]] machine. Around 1950, Hilton took a position at the university maths department. He was there in 1949, when Turing engaged in a discussion that introduced him to the [[word problem for groups]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hodges |first1=Andrew |title=Alan Turing: The Enigma |date=30 November 2012 |publisher=Random House |isbn=978-1-4481-3781-7 |page=412 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EpAl0piM38cC&pg=PA412 |language=en}}</ref> Hilton worked with [[Walter Lederman]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Ledermann |first1=Walter |title=Encounters of a Mathematician |date=1 February 2010 |publisher=Lulu.com |isbn=978-1-4092-8267-9 |page=99 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TngVAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA99 |language=en}}</ref> Another colleague there was [[Hugh Dowker]], who in 1951 drew his attention to the [[Serre spectral sequence]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Dowker |first1=Hugh |title=Aspects of Topology: In Memory of Hugh Dowker 1912-1982 |date=31 January 1985 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-27815-7 |page=281 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=D2k4AAAAIAAJ&pg=PA281 |language=en}}</ref>

In 1952, Hilton moved to [[DPMMS]] in Cambridge, England, where he ran a topology seminar attended by [[John Frank Adams]], [[Michael Atiyah]], [[David B. A. Epstein]], [[Terry Wall]] and [[Christopher Zeeman]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=James |first1=I. M. |title=History of Topology |date=24 August 1999 |publisher=Elsevier |isbn=978-0-08-053407-7 |page=654 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7iRijkz0rrUC&pg=PA654 |language=en}}</ref> Via Hilton, Atiyah became aware of [[Jean-Pierre Serre]]'s [[coherent sheaf]] proof of the [[Riemann–Roch theorem]] for curves, and found his first research direction in sheaf methods for [[ruled surface]]s.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Atiyah |first1=Michael |title=Collected Works: Michael Atiyah Collected Works: Volume 1: Early Papers; General Papers |date=28 April 1988 |publisher=Clarendon Press |isbn=978-0-19-853275-0 |page=2 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YJ0cZwxLECAC&pg=PA1 |language=en}}</ref>

In 1955, Hilton started work with [[Beno Eckmann]] on what became known as [[Eckmann-Hilton duality]] for the [[homotopy category]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Canadian Mathematical Society |title=Canadian Mathematical Bulletin |date=1967 |publisher=Canadian Mathematical Society |page=764 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LMqkjq1z7dMC&pg=PA764 |language=en}}</ref> Through Eckmann, he became editor of the ''[[Ergebnisse der Mathematik und ihrer Grenzgebiete]]'', a position he held from 1964 to 1983.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Götze |first1=Heinz |title=Springer-Verlag: History of a Scientific Publishing House: Part 2: 1945 - 1992. Rebuilding - Opening Frontiers - Securing the Future |date=10 December 2008 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-3-540-92888-1 |page=60 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3f1DAAAAQBAJ&pg=PA60 |language=en}}</ref>

Hilton returned to Manchester as Professor, in 1956.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Otte |first1=M. |title=Mathematiker über die Mathematik |date=8 March 2013 |publisher=Springer-Verlag |isbn=978-3-642-80866-1 |page=426 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PZOfBgAAQBAJ&pg=PA426 |language=de}}</ref> In 1958, he became the Mason Professor of Pure Mathematics at the [[University of Birmingham]].<ref name="bp-about"/> He moved to the United States in 1962 to be Professor of Mathematics at [[Cornell University]], a post he held until 1971.<ref name="all-sorts"/> From 1971 to 1973, he held a joint appointment as Fellow of the Battelle Seattle Research Center and Professor of Mathematics at the University of Washington. On 1 September 1972, he was appointed Louis D. Beaumont University Professor at [[Case Western Reserve University]]; on 1 September 1973, he took up the appointment. In 1982, he was appointed Distinguished Professor of Mathematics at [[Binghamton University]], becoming Emeritus in 2003. Latterly, he spent each spring semester as Distinguished Professor of Mathematics at the [[University of Central Florida]].

Hilton is featured in the book ''Mathematical People''.<ref>D. Albers and [[Gerald L. Alexanderson|G.L. Alexanderson]], Mathematical People, Birkhauser, Boston, 1995. {{isbn|0-8176-3191-7}}</ref>

==Death and family==
Peter Hilton died on  6 November 2010 in [[Binghamton, New York|Binghamton]], [[New York (state)|New York]], at age 87. He left behind his wife, Margaret (born 1925), whom he married in 1949, and their two sons, who were adopted.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Obituaries/Hilton_Telegraph/|title=Professor Peter Hilton – Telegraph obituary|website=mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk|date=November 10, 2010}}</ref> 

Margaret Hilton was a [[Royal Academy of Dramatic Art|RADA]]-trained actress who appeared on Broadway in the shows [[A Day in the Death of Joe Egg]] (1985, [[Longacre Theatre]])<ref>{{Cite web |title=Playbill |url=https://playbill.com/personlistpage/person-list?production=00000150-aea4-d936-a7fd-eef470a60001&type=cp |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260214145232/https://playbill.com/personlistpage/person-list?production=00000150-aea4-d936-a7fd-eef470a60001&type=cp |archive-date=2026-02-14 |access-date=2026-03-18 |website=Playbill |language=en-US}}</ref> and [https://playbill.com/production/rose-cort-theatre-vault-0000003499 Rose] (1980, [[Cort Theatre]]).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Rose (Broadway, Cort Theatre, 1981) |url=https://playbill.com/production/rose-cort-theatre-vault-0000003499 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251109193910/https://playbill.com/production/rose-cort-theatre-vault-0000003499 |archive-date=2025-11-09 |access-date=2026-03-18 |website=Playbill |language=en-US}}</ref> In 1978 she won the [[Clarence Derwent Awards#1970s 2|Actors Equity Association's award]] for the most promising actress on the New York stage, for her role in [https://www.nytimes.com/1978/01/23/archives/molly-a-melodrama-by-simon-gray-with-tammy-grimes.html Molly].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Clarence Derwent Award |url=https://www.actorsequityfoundation.org/clarence-derwent-award |access-date=2026-03-18 |website=Actors' Equity Foundation |language=en-US}}</ref> She also played television roles.<ref>{{cite web |title=Margaret Hilton |url=https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0385285 |website=IMDb}}</ref> She died in [[Seattle]] in 2020.<ref>{{cite web |title=Margaret Hilton Obituary - Seattle, WA |url=https://www.dignitymemorial.com/obituaries/seattle-wa/margaret-hilton-9864159 |website=Dignity Memorial |language=en}}</ref>

==In popular culture==
Hilton is portrayed by actor [[Matthew Beard (English actor)|Matthew Beard]] in the 2014 film ''[[The Imitation Game]]'', which tells the tale of [[Alan Turing]] and the cracking of [[Nazi Germany]]'s [[Enigma code]].

==Academic positions==
* Lecturer at [[University of Cambridge]], 1952–55
* Senior Lecturer at [[Victoria University of Manchester|University of Manchester]], England, 1956–58
* Mason Professor of Pure Mathematics, [[University of Birmingham]], England, 1958–62
* Visiting Professor at the Eidgenössische Technische Hochschule at Zürich, [[ETH Zurich]], 1966–67, 1981–82, 1988–89
* Visiting Professor at the [[Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences]], New York University, 1967–68
* Visiting Professor at the Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona, [[Autonomous University of Barcelona]], 1989
* Professeur invité, [[University of Lausanne]], in 1996

==Honours==
* Silver Medal, [[University of Helsinki]], 1975
* Doctor of Humanities (hon. causa), N. [[University of Michigan]], 1977
* Corresponding Member, [[Brazilian Academy of Sciences]], 1979
* Doctor of Science (hon. causa), [[Memorial University of Newfoundland]], 1983
* Doctor of Science (hon. causa), [[Autonomous University of Barcelona]], 1989
* In August 1983, an international conference on algebraic topology was held, under the auspices of the Canadian Mathematical Society, to mark Hilton's 60th Birthday. Professor Hilton was presented with a Festschrift of papers dedicated to him ([[London Mathematical Society]] Lecture Notes, Volume 86, 1983). The [[American Mathematical Society]] has published the proceedings under the title ‘Conference on Algebraic Topology in Honor of Peter Hilton’<ref>Contemporary Mathematics 37, AMS, 1985</ref>
* Hilton was selected in October 1992, to deliver the invited lecture at the ‘Georges de Rham’ day at the [[University of Lausanne]].
* An International Conference was held in Montreal in May 1993, to mark the 70th birthday of Hilton. The proceedings were published as The Hilton Symposium, CRM Proceedings and Lecture Notes, Volume 6, American Mathematical Society (1994), edited by [[Guido Mislin]].
* In 1994, Hilton was the Mahler Lecturer of the Australian Mathematical Society.
* In the summers of 2001 and 2002, Hilton was Visiting Erskine Fellow at the University of Canterbury, Christchurch, New Zealand.<ref>{{cite web |title=Philosophy |url=https://www.canterbury.ac.nz/engage/erskine/roll/department/philosophy/ |website=The University of Canterbury |language=en-nz |access-date=14 August 2021 |archive-date=7 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221007164617/https://www.canterbury.ac.nz/engage/erskine/roll/department/philosophy/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>
* In winter term of 2005 Hilton received an appointment as Courtesy Faculty in the College of Arts and Sciences at University of South Florida.

==Hilton's former PhD students==
According to the [[Mathematics Genealogy Project]] site, Hilton supervised at least 27 doctoral students, including [[Paul Chester Kainen|Paul Kainen]] at Cornell University.<ref name="mathgen"/>
